planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Banilejo is a vigorous, heavy-cropping dooryard mango that handles the humid lowland heat of the southern Dominican coast well.

directions: Banilejo takes its name from the city of Baní in the Dominican Republic's Peravia province, where it has long been the region's signature dooryard and smallholder mango and a major source of fruit for domestic markets and ethnic export trade. The fruit is comparatively small, turning a reddish-yellow blush at ripeness, with notably sweet, deeply aromatic flesh and an early-to-midseason harvest window that lets growers get fruit to market ahead of many larger-fruited commercial types. Trees are productive and reliable bearers even on marginal, dry hillside soils typical of the Baní area, making this a practical choice where irrigation is limited. Give it full sun, a well-drained site, and the same wet-dry seasonal rhythm it experiences in its home region, and expect a tree that crops dependably once established.
sources: FAO AGRIS: Characterization of mango 'Banilejo' for commercial exploitation in the Dominican Republic
Agronometrics Dominican Republic mango export reporting

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Limaní is one of Puerto Rico's own bred coffees and is grown almost exclusively on the island's mountain farms.

directions: Limaní was bred at Puerto Rico's agricultural experiment station in Adjuntas from a cross of Timor Hybrid and Villa Sarchí, and released to farmers in 1994 specifically to give the island's growers a cultivar able to shrug off coffee leaf rust (roya), which was devastating older Typica and Bourbon plantings. It takes its name from the Limaní neighborhood of Adjuntas where the breeding work was centered, and today it is grown almost nowhere else in the world outside Puerto Rico. Plants are compact and productive, tolerating the lower-elevation, warmer sites common across the island's coffee belt better than older heirloom lines. Grow it as any shade-loving Arabica, with dappled light, steady moisture, and acidic, humus-rich soil, and expect the first cherries roughly three to four years after planting.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez Agricultural Experiment Station (Estación Experimental Agrícola, Adjuntas)
World Coffee Research Variety Catalog: Frontón/Limaní
Puerto Rico Coffee Shop Encyclopedia: Limaní and Frontón

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Frontón was bred for Puerto Rico's lower and middle elevations and tolerates warmer sites than older heirloom Arabica types.

directions: Frontón is a cross of Timor Hybrid and Caturra selected at Puerto Rico's Adjuntas experiment station using breeding material originally sourced from Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas, and it takes its name from the Frontón neighborhood of Ciales where the selection work was carried out. Released alongside its sibling cultivar Limaní around the late 1980s and early 1990s, it was bred specifically to resist coffee leaf rust while still cropping heavily at the lower, warmer elevations where many Puerto Rican smallholders farm. It is an early, high-yielding plant that bears sooner after planting than many older Typica or Bourbon lines. Treat it like other shade-tolerant Arabica cultivars, with partial shade, consistent moisture, and rich acidic soil, and expect a comparatively quick and heavy first harvest.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez Agricultural Experiment Station (Adjuntas)
World Coffee Research Variety Catalog: Frontón
Puerto Rico Coffee Shop Encyclopedia: Limaní and Frontón

planting.note: Plant a sword sucker or tissue-culture plantlet in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Maricongo is the dominant commercial plantain clone of Puerto Rico.

directions: Maricongo is a horn-type plantain clone that accounts for roughly nine out of every ten plantains grown commercially in Puerto Rico, and it is also widely grown across the Dominican Republic as a staple cooking banana. Bunches carry large, elongated fingers with green skin that turns yellow as they ripen, and the pulp stays firm and starchy even when fully ripe, which is exactly why cooks prize it for tostones, mofongo, and other fried or boiled preparations rather than eating it raw. The plant is a vigorous grower that benefits from generous spacing, deep fertile soil, and steady irrigation through fruit fill, since yields can be inconsistent under stress despite good bunch and finger size when conditions are favorable. Remove excess suckers to leave one follower per mat, mulch heavily to conserve moisture, and expect bunches roughly ten to fourteen months after planting.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Journal of Agriculture: 'Effect of Planting Pattern and Population Density on Yield and Quality of the Horn-Type Maricongo Plantain'
USDA Agricultural Research Service, Tropical Agriculture Research Station, Mayagüez
ResearchGate: Behavior of plantain clones Maricongo and FHIA-21 under black Sigatoka

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Semil 34 is a large, late-producing tree and is the backbone of the Dominican Republic's avocado export industry.

directions: Semil 34 arose as a chance seedling of mixed Guatemalan and West Indian parentage found on the Semil plantation in Villalba, Puerto Rico, around the late 1940s, and growers later carried grafted material from Puerto Rico into the Dominican Republic, where it has since become the country's single most widely planted avocado, making up roughly two-thirds of commercial orchards. The tree is large and spreading, a heavy but notably late bearer, and carries large, pear-shaped fruit with a snugly seated seed that resists bruising in transit, a trait that has made it the backbone of the Dominican fresh-export trade. It needs full sun and a deep, well-drained site to support its size, and like other A-flower-type avocados benefits from a nearby B-type pollinizer for best fruit set. Expect a slow trip to first bearing and then a reliably heavy, late-season harvest once the tree matures.
sources: Specialty Produce: Semil 34 Avocado variety profile
MDPI Applied Sciences: Characterization of Avocado Seed Extract from the Variety Semil 34 Cultivated in the Dominican Republic
